People always ask me what the hardest part of an inquiry is. It is not finding the evidence. It is deciding which question you are actually answering.
In this case the question looked obvious from the outside. Why did the city go dark?
And that is exactly the wrong question. What we should have asked in month one was why nine minutes passed between the alarm and the disconnection.

Good afternoon. I want to set out what we know one week on. At eleven minutes past two on Tuesday morning, an alarm was recorded at the substation. At fourteen minutes past two, the main transformer disconnected, and within six minutes approximately four hundred thousand customers had lost supply. The cause, on the evidence available to us today, was a storm of a severity that this equipment was not designed to withstand. I am aware that questions have been raised about the interval between the alarm and the disconnection, and that interval is being reviewed. A full report will be published within ninety days. Nothing will be withheld from it. I will take three questions.

The log is not complicated. It is one page. There was an inspection due the previous March, and it was postponed, and then it was postponed again, and then it simply is not there any more. I raised it twice. I was told it was a scheduling matter and not my department, which, I mean, technically that is correct. And I let it go, and that is the part I think about. What I still cannot tell you, two years on, is who took it off the calendar. The system that would have recorded that was replaced in January, and nobody kept the old one. So the honest answer is that we know what happened and we do not know who decided it, and I would rather say that plainly than pretend otherwise.
